strengths: The paper addresses an important question: why categorical distributional RL can outperform expectation-based RL. Its conditional cross-entropy decomposition offers a potentially useful perspective for investigating this difference.

The experiments provide substantial coverage, including eight Atari games, several continuous-control environments, three or five seeds, interpolation-weight sensitivity, and comparisons involving C51 and IQN. The environment-dependent interaction between policy entropy and distributional critics is a useful empirical observation.

The manuscript discusses relevant foundational work, provides algorithm pseudocode and common hyperparameters, and explicitly acknowledges the theoretical gap between categorical and quantile-based methods. No material ethical concerns are apparent from the reported simulation studies.
weaknesses: The central DERAC derivation is incorrect. In Appendix I, Eq. 36, writing δ = T^π Q_{θ*} − Q_θ, expanding (δ + √(τH))² gives δ² + τH + 2√τ δ√H. The displayed cross term has the wrong form, and its removal is unjustified: Bellman-residual orthogonality does not generally hold for arbitrary learned critics and lagged target networks. Consequently, Eq. 10 is not established as the squared residual of the proposed augmented Bellman operator.

The loss decomposition does not establish the claimed exploration mechanism. Proposition 4.3 gives, at most, agreement of limiting fitted targets under sufficiently expressive models and vanishing bin width. It does not establish equivalence between finite-bin neural cross-entropy training and squared-error FQI, including their gradients and approximation errors. Introducing the reward bonus in Eq. 7 therefore requires an additional argument connecting it to ordinary CDRL policy updates.

The convergence guarantees do not adequately address the proposed coupled learning process. Appendix H uses standard policy-evaluation and improvement arguments that require the augmented reward to remain fixed. Here, the bonus depends on the learned critic and policy-dependent return targets. Bounded cross-entropy alone does not justify treating this changing bonus as a stationary reward. Freezing these quantities would establish a substantially narrower result.

Cross-entropy is not purely a measure of distribution mismatch: H(μ,q) = H(μ) + KL(μ||q). Even when q perfectly matches μ, the proposed bonus retains the target entropy. Thus, a large bonus can reflect irreducible return randomness rather than an estimate lagging behind its target. This undermines the stated interpretation of exploration directed toward insufficiently learned states.

Additional mathematical issues weaken the theoretical support. If the mean bin has zero probability, Proposition 4.1 forces ϵ = 1, making α = ϵ/(1−ϵ) undefined. For continuous targets, shrinking the bins also forces ϵ toward one, which needs reconciliation with the limiting argument. Furthermore, Appendix G's claimed o(Δ) convergence rate is incorrect: Eq. 32 gives an error between Δ/4 and Δ/2, hence Θ(Δ).

The experiments demonstrate performance changes but do not isolate their cause. Replacing the full target distribution with the residual distribution changes the learning target, while switching between scalar and distributional critics changes representation and optimization. Return curves alone cannot distinguish exploration benefits from these effects. Controlled uncertainty experiments and direct measurements of visitation or estimation error are needed to support the central explanation; interpolation curves also cannot substantiate the tabular convergence theorem.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the supplied pseudocode and hyperparameters. The manuscript does not precisely specify the experimental ε-to-ϵ mapping and mass-redistribution procedure, categorical support ranges, Atari-specific configuration, or the meaning of shaded uncertainty bands. No implementation link for the proposed modifications is provided.
